vignette:
Marguerite is a seventy-nine-year-old widowed woman of French descent who works part-time as a tailor out of a small alterations shop she has kept for decades in her neighborhood. She came to the clinic after her daughter, increasingly alarmed by her mother's withdrawal, made the appointment on her behalf. What Marguerite carried into the intake session was not easily spoken - it rarely has been, she said, for more than sixty years.

As a young woman in her late teens, Marguerite witnessed the aftermath of a military assault on her village in rural France. She had been helping her father in his shop when the sounds began. What she saw when she stepped outside - a neighbor's body, the blood pooling dark and wide across the pale stone - became the image that would never fully form into language and never fully leave. The sequence of what happened that afternoon remains fractured: she knows certain things occurred, but the order collapses whenever she tries to reconstruct it, and the attempt to put the experience into words produces only a kind of blankness, a sense that language itself is inadequate to what she endured. When the memories do surface - unbidden, incomplete - what rises with them is not grief but rage, a white and wordless fury that frightens her with its intensity.

The triggers that pull her back are specific and merciless. Unwanted thoughts intrude without warning, often while she is working at her sewing table - the quiet rhythm of stitching offering no real protection. Certain conversation topics, especially anything touching on war, soldiers, or violence in the news, can send her back within seconds. And blood - even a small cut on a customer's finger, a stain on fabric brought in for repair - is enough to collapse the distance between then and now. Each time a trigger fires, it does not merely recall the past; it confirms her darkest present-tense conviction: that nothing good can happen to her anymore, that the person she once was - someone capable of happiness - is simply gone. The triggers, in this way, do not only retrieve the trauma; they actively reinforce the belief that she is beyond recovery, and that belief, in turn, keeps her hypervigilant to anything that might provoke the memories again, narrowing her world further with each cycle.

The memories themselves, fragmented and nonverbal as they are, have quietly shaped the architecture of her daily life. Because she cannot organize what happened into a coherent narrative, the past remains unresolved and present, a wound without edges. This unprocessed quality feeds directly into her conviction that she is permanently changed - emotionally dead, she said, in a flat voice that seemed to confirm the claim. And from that conviction, a particular logic has taken hold: if she allows herself to feel something good, she will only lose it again. So she has learned, over decades, to preempt that loss. She avoids situations that might bring pleasure or hope. When warmth arises - a kind word from a customer, a moment of sunlight through the shop window - she pushes it away before it can settle, because positive emotion has come to feel like a trap. She has stopped seeing friends. The social world that once sustained her has contracted to almost nothing, and the isolation this produces circles back to deepen her certainty that she is miserable and will remain so - that the woman who used to laugh, who used to feel, is irretrievable.

Marguerite's grief over who she used to be is quiet but total. She does not cry easily. She describes herself as feeling dead inside with the matter-of-fact tone of someone reporting the weather. What finally brought her to seek help was not a crisis but an accumulation: her daughter's face at Christmas, the recognition that she had not been present at her own granddaughter's wedding in any meaningful way, the understanding that she had been disappearing for a very long time. What she fears most is that it is too late. What she hopes, in the smallest and most guarded part of herself, is that someone might tell her otherwise.
